《三國史記》（1146）記載，伽倻琴約於六世紀在伽倻聯盟由嘉悉王依中國古箏發展，: The Samguk Sagi (1146) records that the gayageum was developed around the sixth century in the Gaya confederacy by King Gasil on the model of the Chinese guzheng, and that Ureuk was ordered to compose for it; Ureuk later improved it in the reign of King Jinheung of Silla. Other archaeological material indicates that fragments from about the first century BCE have been excavated in the Jeolla region. Around the eighth century it reached Japan by way of Silla, and the Shōsōin holds a Silla-style zither; at the end of the nineteenth century it reached the Korean communities of China. The early twelve-string instrument was mostly used for aak, and later, as sanjo rose, the body was shortened and the strings brought closer together. From the 1960s modern gayageum enlarged the soundbox and increased the count to eighteen, twenty-one or twenty-five strings.

Sound is made by the right hand plucking and flicking the strings near the bridge, usually mainly with the index finger; the left hand presses the strings to the left of the bridges to raise the pitch and add vibrato and ornaments. A beginner can first practise the sitting position and the support of the tail, then the right-hand plucking and the left-hand pressing, adjusting to the speed of the piece: jeongak is slower, while sanjo needs faster passages.

The old form had a body hollowed from a single block of paulownia (tong wood) into a resonating trough; on sanjo instruments the soundboard is paulownia and the sides and back are hardwoods such as chestnut or walnut. The frame and the bridges are padauk or rosewood, and the bottom board is chestnut. The traditional strings are silk, and in modern times there are nylon strings, nylon-wound steel strings and brass strings. The materials of the movable bridges, tuning pegs, bridges and feet are not stated.

The jeongak gayageum can accompany court music, chamber music and songs, and plays slow pieces such as "Yeongsan hoesang"; the sanjo gayageum is used for sanjo solos, usually accompanied by the janggu, with the tempo running from slow to fast. Today it also appears in solos, duos, ensembles and sung performance, and in concertos with orchestra such as Hwang Byung Ki's "Forest" and Beomhoon Park's "New Sanjo".

Traditionally it has twelve strings, and modern instruments add more to widen the range; there is no single standard tuning, and it can be adjusted to use. The volume depends on the construction of the body: the old form has no bottom board and is quieter; adding a bottom board to make a resonating box increases the volume, and modern instruments enlarge the soundbox and use nylon or nylon-wound steel strings to make the sound fuller. Compared with relatives such as the Chinese guzheng and the Japanese koto, the right-hand plucking and left-hand pressing are similar, but sanjo playing on the gayageum usually uses closer string spacing and a shorter body, and the left hand presses and vibrates over a wider range, so the timbre is soft, fine and subtle.

The gayageum is a traditional plucked instrument of the Korean peninsula, of the zither family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 312.22-5. It traditionally has twelve strings, with later variants of thirteen, seventeen, eighteen, twenty-one, twenty-two and twenty-five strings; there is one bridge per string, and the bridges can be moved to tune. The body uses paulownia or fish-scale pine for the soundboard, and some forms add a bottom board and hardwood sides and back. It is played with the right hand plucking on the near side of the bridges and the left hand pressing the strings to raise the pitch and add vibrato, and it can be played sitting on the floor or on a chair. Musicians of the Korean peninsula use it for traditional music, court music, chamber music, lyric song, sanjo and folk music, as a solo instrument, in duos, in ensembles or in sung performance.
